h1: Renovating an Old School Playground: Repair, Replace or Rebuild?

props.title: Renovating an Old School Playground: Repair, Replace or Rebuild?
props.summaryText: Many schools have a playground that is tired rather than new. How to assess what you have, decide what to keep, repair or replace, and phase the work around the school calendar.
props.author: priya-nair
props.imageAlt: School children running and playing outdoors

takeaways.text: Start with an inspection: list every item, its condition and whether spares are available.
Repair what is structurally sound; replace what is corroded at the base, cracked or unsafe by design.
The surface is often the biggest upgrade: replacing concrete or worn soil with a safe surface changes everything.
Phase the work during school holidays and keep part of the playground open if possible.

faq.q: How do I know if old playground equipment should be replaced?
faq.a: Replace equipment with structural corrosion at the base of posts or welds, cracked or brittle plastic, parts that cannot be repaired or sourced, or a design that creates hazards such as head entrapment gaps or very high platforms without barriers. Equipment that is sound but tired can often be repaired and refreshed.

faq.q: Can old playground equipment be repaired?
faq.a: Often, yes. Loose fixings, worn swing seats and chains, damaged bolt caps and surface rust can be fixed. Some plastic parts can be replaced if the manufacturer still supplies them. A qualified inspection tells you what is worth repairing.

faq.q: When is the best time to renovate a school playground?
faq.a: During the long summer holidays, so foundations can cure and surfaces can be laid without children on site and before the monsoon. Shorter breaks can be used for smaller phases.
